title: "Updates on Imaging Assessment of Pancreatic Cancer"

format: revealjs

## Background: PDAC Lethality
- Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal malignancy
- Reported five-year survival rate of approximately 10%
- Complete surgical resection is the only potentially curative treatment
- Only 20% of newly diagnosed patients present with early-stage disease amenable to curative-intent resection

## Evolution of Treatment Paradigms
- Introduction of multiagent chemotherapy regimens has changed management
- Neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) increasingly adopted as initial treatment
- Expectation of improving surgical candidacy through conversion surgery
- Goal of enhancing oncological outcomes in borderline and locally advanced disease

## Central Role of Imaging
- Imaging evaluation plays a central role in clinical decision-making
- Pancreatic CT protocol remains the cornerstone for clinical staging
- CT is the preferred first-line modality for assessing anatomical resectability
- MRI and 18F-FDG PET/CT serve as valuable problem-solving tools

## Limitations of Anatomical Resectability
- High rate of recurrence after surgical resection even among anatomically resectable cases
- Highlights limitations of treatment decisions based on anatomy alone
- Emergence of biological resectability concept
- Integration of imaging, laboratory, and biological biomarkers reflecting tumor aggressiveness

## Restaging After Neoadjuvant Therapy
- Patients initially treated with NAT require reassessment for curative resection
- Radiological restaging is more challenging than initial staging
- Imaging cannot reliably differentiate viable tumors from post-treatment fibrosis
- Various approaches proposed to address these restaging challenges

## Overview of Imaging Techniques
- High-quality dedicated imaging of the pancreas required at initial presentation and at restaging
- Most guidelines recommend pancreatic protocol CT or MRI as standard
- Pancreatic protocol CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the preferred modality
- Some guidelines also recommend chest CT for complete staging

## Pancreatic CT Protocol: Technical Requirements
- Multidetector CT scanners preferably with 64 or more detector rows
- Thin detector collimation for high spatial resolution
- Rapid intravenous contrast injection at 3 to 5 mL per second
- Dual-phase imaging consisting of pancreatic and portal venous phases

## Pancreatic Phase CT Imaging
- Recommended scan time 40 to 50 seconds after intravenous contrast injection per NCCN
- Many institutions employ bolus-tracking techniques to optimize timing
- Provides maximal contrast between hypovascular tumor and enhanced normal parenchyma
- Facilitates tumor detection and assessment of tumor contact with major arteries

## Portal Venous Phase CT Imaging
- Recommended scan time 65 to 70 seconds after contrast injection per NCCN
- Optimal phase for evaluating venous tumor involvement
- Best for assessing adjacent organ invasion
- Preferred phase for detection of liver metastases

## Delayed Phase CT Imaging
- Performed in addition to biphasic imaging in some institutions
- May improve detection of PDAC that appears isoattenuating on biphasic imaging
- Particularly useful for revealing tumors not visible on standard dual-phase protocols
- Optional but valuable problem-solving component

## CT Image Reconstruction and Review
- Images should be reconstructed using thin sections preferably 2 to 3 mm
- Multiplanar reconstruction is strongly recommended
- Coronal images should be routinely reviewed at a minimum
- Critical for accurate assessment of tumor-vessel contact and anatomic variations

## MRI: Role as a Problem-Solving Tool
- Commonly used for identifying suspicious PDACs not clearly visible on CT
- Particularly valuable for detecting hepatic metastasis
- Accuracy of MRI for local tumor staging reported as comparable to CT
- Offers distinct advantage in detecting small liver metastases

## MRI Protocol for PDAC Assessment
- Non-enhanced axial T1- and T2-weighted imaging
- Diffusion-weighted imaging
- T2-weighted MR cholangiopancreatography
- Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging during pancreatic, portal venous, and delayed phases with thin sections

## MRI for Hepatic Metastases Detection
- Meta-analyses demonstrate higher sensitivity than CT for liver metastases from PDAC
- Similar specificity maintained compared to CT
- Hepatobiliary phase imaging improves lesion conspicuity
- Diffusion-weighted imaging particularly valuable for detecting minute metastases

## 18F-FDG PET/CT: Staging Role
- Not routinely recommended for initial PDAC staging
- May be useful for detection of occult distant metastasis
- Consider in patients with non-metastatic disease on routine CT who exhibit high-risk features
- Indicated for markedly elevated CA 19-9, large primary tumors, or suspicious lymph nodes

## PET/CT for Tumor Biology Assessment
- Gained attention as a tool for predicting tumor aggressiveness
- Provides quantitative information on tumor metabolic activity
- Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) serves as potential biomarker
- Useful for assessing treatment response in patients receiving NAT

## Imaging Assessment at Initial Diagnosis
- Comprehensive imaging assessment required for all patients with suspected or known PDAC
- Must evaluate distant metastasis and tumor resectability
- Lymph node status and extra-pancreatic organ involvement assessed
- Anatomic variations and other management-affecting findings documented

## SAR and APA Consensus Statement
- Published in 2014 by Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association
- Standardized terminology for radiology reporting in PDAC
- Outlined essential components for systematic imaging assessment
- Facilitates multidisciplinary discussion and consistent communication

## Assessment of Tumor-Vessel Contact
- For non-metastatic PDAC, resectability primarily determined by major vessel involvement
- Major vessels include celiac artery, hepatic artery, superior mesenteric artery
- Also includes variant arteries, portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, and inferior vena cava
- Degree of contact classified into three main categories

## Classification: No Contact
- Defined as a preserved fat plane between the tumor and the vessel
- Indicates absence of pathological vessel invasion
- Best negative predictive value for excluding vascular invasion
- Favorable prognostic indicator for resection

## Classification: Abutment
- Defined as solid tumor contact involving 180 degrees or less of vessel circumference
- Further divided into abutment without vessel deformity
- And abutment with deformity based on contour irregularities
- Less specific than encasement for true invasion

## Classification: Encasement
- Defined as solid tumor contact involving greater than 180 degrees of vessel circumference
- Highly predictive of true arterial invasion
- High specificity and positive predictive value
- Indicates advanced local disease often precluding straightforward resection

## Additional Vascular Reporting Elements
- Presence of vessel stenosis, obstruction, or thrombosis should be explicitly reported
- Tumor extension to the first branch of SMA and SMV documented
- Involvement of jejunal branches of SMA may affect resectability
- Degree of contact associated with perivascular haziness also recommended

## Perivascular Haziness Significance
- May be observed after chemotherapy or radiation therapy
- Reflects replacement of solid tumor by fibrosis, inflammation, or residual viable tumor
- Can also occur in concomitant pancreatitis
- Important context for interpreting post-treatment imaging

## Arterial Variants: Clinical Importance
- Aberrant right or common hepatic arteries arising from SMA are particularly important
- Especially relevant in pancreatic head PDAC
- These variant arteries typically traverse the portocaval space
- Therefore highly susceptible to involvement by pancreatic head cancers

## Figure 2: Replaced Right Hepatic Artery
- 77-year-old man with pancreatic head cancer
- Axial arterial-phase CT images of two consecutive sections shown
- Hypodense pancreatic head mass (arrowheads) visible
- Replaced right hepatic artery (small arrows) arises from SMA (large arrow)
- Artery traverses portocaval space posterior to pancreatic head

## Perineural Tumor Spread: Definition
- Pancreatic head PDACs may extend along extra-pancreatic neural plexuses
- Surrounding peripancreatic vasculature
- Referred to as perineural tumor spread
- Distinct pattern of local invasion with major surgical implications

## Perineural Spread Pathways and Imaging
- On CT and MRI manifests as soft-tissue extension from primary tumor
- Extends along inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery toward SMA
- Along gastroduodenal artery toward celiac artery
- Extends posteriorly from pancreatic head

## Figure 3: Extensive Perineural Spread
- 65-year-old man with small 1.5-cm pancreatic head tumor
- Axial T1-weighted MR shows mass with lower signal intensity (arrow)
- CT shows soft-tissue extension (arrowheads) toward SMA (arrow)
- Coronal CT reveals solid infiltration encasing both celiac artery and SMA
- Demonstrates extensive spread despite small primary tumor size

## Surgical Significance: Portal Vein Involvement
- Nakao et al. classified radiological PV involvement into four grades
- Categories: absent, unilateral narrowing, bilateral narrowing, stenosis or obstruction
- PV resection performed in 19.8%, 93.9%, 99.0%, and 100% respectively
- Pathological PV wall invasion present in 0%, 51%, 74%, and 93%

## Surgical Significance: Vein Contact Categories
- Tran Cao et al. reported consistent findings in upfront resection cohort
- Vein resection required in 11.1% with no contact, 25.0% with abutment, 100% with encasement
- Pathologic vein invasion present in 3.7%, 16.1%, and 100% respectively
- Absence of contact indicates absence of invasion; encasement indicates high likelihood

## Arterial Invasion: Optimal CT Threshold
- Noda et al. evaluated tumor-vessel contact in 128 patients with PDAC
- Any solid tumor contact: sensitivity 100%, specificity 93%, NPV 100%
- Optimal threshold for detecting arterial invasion
- Excellent negative predictive value for excluding arterial involvement

## Arterial Encasement Specificity
- Solid tumor contact greater than 180 degrees: specificity 97% to 99%
- Positive predictive value 44% to 67% for arterial invasion
- Another study of 105 patients: sensitivity 88%, specificity 94%, NPV 99%
- Arterial encasement highly predictive; abutment sensitive but less specific

## Anatomical Tumor Resectability: NCCN Criteria
- NCCN criteria most widely used for assessing anatomical resectability
- Non-metastatic PDAC categorized as resectable, borderline resectable, or locally advanced
- Based primarily on extent of tumor-vessel contact
- Determines likelihood of achieving margin-negative R0 resection

## Resectable Disease Criteria
- No tumor contact with major arteries
- No tumor contact with major veins, or venous abutment without deformity
- Associated with highest probability of R0 resection
- Traditional standard for upfront surgical resection

## Borderline Resectable: Venous Criteria
- Tumor abutment with deformity or encasement of major veins
- Includes portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, and inferior vena cava
- Must be amenable to safe venous resection and reconstruction
- Limited longitudinal extent without extensive branch vessel involvement

## Borderline Resectable: Arterial Criteria
- Pancreatic head tumors with abutment of common hepatic artery, SMA, or variant hepatic artery
- Pancreatic body or tail tumors with abutment of celiac artery
- Short-segment common hepatic artery involvement without extension to celiac artery or bifurcation
- Tumor involvement at gastroduodenal artery root equivalent to hepatic artery involvement

## Borderline Resectable Subclassification
- BR-PV defined as portal vein or superior mesenteric vein involvement alone
- BR-A defined as arterial involvement of any major artery
- Rationale: BR-A tumors associated with worse prognosis
- Greater risk of incomplete resection and increased perioperative morbidity

## Locally Advanced Disease: Definition
- Extensive involvement of major vessels precluding complete surgical resection
- Includes encasement of superior mesenteric artery or celiac artery
- Tumor involvement of both celiac artery and abdominal aorta
- Unreconstructible portal vein-superior mesenteric vein involvement

## Figure 5: Hepatic Artery Involvement as Locally Advanced
- 66-year-old woman with pancreatic head cancer
- Coronal CT shows mass encasing gastroduodenal artery and involving common hepatic artery
- Anatomic variation with short proper hepatic artery
- Left and right hepatic arteries arise directly from common hepatic artery
- Required hepatic artery resection and ligation; postoperative hepatic infarction resulted

## Figure 6A-B: SMA Encasement with SMV Stenosis
- Axial arterial-phase and coronal portal venous-phase MIP images
- Hypodense pancreatic head mass with SMV abutment and deformity (small arrow)
- Superior mesenteric artery encasement (large arrow)
- MIP clearly depicts SMV stenosis
- Locally advanced due to arterial encasement

## Figure 6C-D: Long-Segment Unreconstructible Vein Involvement
- Axial portal venous-phase and coronal ray-sum images
- Pancreatic head mass with SMV abutment and deformity (small arrows)
- SMA abutment (large arrows)
- Coronal image shows long-segment involvement of SMV and tributaries
- Dashed lines indicate estimated extent; considered locally advanced

## Figure 7: Appleby Procedure for Celiac Axis Resection
- 65-year-old woman with pancreatic body cancer
- Preoperative CT shows tumor encasing common hepatic artery with extension to celiac artery
- Patent superior mesenteric artery and gastroduodenal artery without involvement
- Postoperative CT shows clips ligating celiac artery at origin
- Distal pancreatectomy with celiac artery resection performed successfully

## Lymph Node Metastasis: Imaging Features
- Suspicious features include short-axis diameter greater than 1 cm
- Abnormal round morphology
- Heterogeneity or central necrosis
- Location within lymphatic drainage pathways of primary tumor

## Lymph Node Metastasis: Regional vs Distant
- Only lymph nodes within surgical resection boundaries considered regional
- Lymph node metastases beyond surgical fields classified as distant metastases
- CT and MRI have limited sensitivity for detecting nodal metastasis
- Reported CT sensitivity 23.5% and specificity 89.9%

## PET/CT for Lymph Node Assessment
- May complement CT or MRI in detecting metastatic lymph nodes
- Standalone PET/CT also has limited sensitivity
- Combined contrast-enhanced CT and PET/CT yields low sensitivity of 22.4% to 32.0%
- Despite limited sensitivity, suspicious nodes are consistently adverse prognostic factor

## Adjacent Organ Invasion: General Principles
- Technically resectable extra-pancreatic organ invasion not a determinant of PDAC resectability
- Invasion necessitates additional resection and modified surgical approach
- Particularly concerning in pancreatic tail tumors
- Less likely to involve major vessels but more frequently invade adjacent organs

## Adjacent Organ Invasion in Tail Tumors
- Commonly invades spleen, stomach, colon, jejunum, kidney, and adrenal gland
- Solid tumor contact with adjacent organs with or without contour deformity
- Optimal CT criterion: sensitivity 91.2% and specificity 96.0%
- Technically resectable invasion does not adversely affect margin status or survival

## Figure 8: Tail Cancer with Central Necrosis and Organ Invasion
- 65-year-old man with pancreatic tail mass
- Central necrosis appearing as non-enhancing area within tumor
- Maximal dimension 4.5 cm; CA 19-9 markedly elevated at 2,216 U/mL
- Coronal CT shows suspected invasion of stomach and proximal jejunum
- Pathology revealed undifferentiated carcinoma of sarcomatoid type

## Celiac Artery and SMA Stenosis: Recognition
- Important in patients undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy
- Arterial perfusion of hepatic, gastric, and mesenteric circulations may depend on collaterals
- Pancreaticoduodenal arcade typically resected during procedure
- Unrecognized stenosis may lead to hepatic, gastric, or mesenteric ischemia

## Figure 9: Nonocclusive Mesenteric Ischemia
- 74-year-old woman after pancreaticoduodenectomy for IPMN
- Severe stenosis at superior mesenteric artery orifice
- Celiac artery and gastroduodenal artery enlarged as collateral pathway
- Postoperative CT shows ileus and decreased enhancement of ileum and ascending colon
- Due to mesenteric hypoperfusion after loss of collateral perfusion

## Biological and Conditional Factors: Introduction
- Achieving margin-negative resection has traditionally been the primary surgical goal
- High recurrence rates persist even after R0 resection in anatomically resectable disease
- One-year recurrence-free survival only 45% after upfront resection for resectable PDAC
- 49% even among those achieving R0 resection

## Biological Resectability Concept
- Emphasizes consideration of high-risk features suggesting aggressive tumor biology
- Goes beyond anatomic tumor extent alone
- Integration of imaging, laboratory, and biological biomarkers
- Patients with resectable anatomy but high-risk features may be better classified as borderline resectable

## Potential Biological Factors
- Serum carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels
- Imaging tumor phenotype and morphological characteristics
- Lymph node status
- Metabolic activity on 18F-FDG PET/CT expressed as SUVmax

## Conditional Factors
- Host-related factors associated with postoperative morbidity and mortality risk
- Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status most commonly used
- Modified Glasgow prognostic score
- Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio
- Onodera prognostic nutritional index

## A-B-C Approach to Clinical Staging
- A: Anatomical resectability
- B: Biologic factors such as CA 19-9 level greater than 500 U/mL
- C: Patient condition such as ECOG performance status
- Provides better survival stratification than anatomical resectability alone
- Validated in cohort treated with modified FOLFIRINOX

## Imaging Phenotype: Delta Metric
- Koay et al. reported quantitative delta metric on CT
- Represents degree of enhancement difference between tumor and surrounding parenchyma
- Conspicuous tumors with high delta values associated with lower stromal content
- Higher prevalence of common pathway mutations, early metastasis, and shorter survival

## Imaging Phenotype: Necrosis and Rim Enhancement
- Tumors exhibiting necrosis on CT associated with poor prognosis
- Rim enhancement at MRI predicts aggressive pathological features
- Includes poor differentiation and lymph node metastasis
- Contrast with favorable features such as isoattenuation on CT

## Favorable Imaging Features
- Visually isoattenuating tumors on CT suggested as favorable prognostic feature
- Larger extracellular volume reflected by increased equilibrium-phase enhancement
- Suggests less aggressive underlying tumor biology
- Important counterpoints to necrosis and rim enhancement markers

## Serum CA 19-9: Prognostic Value
- Tumor-associated antigen most widely used to assess PDAC
- Pretreatment level correlated with tumor stage and survival outcomes
- Relevant for both surgical resection and chemotherapy outcomes
- Enables prognostic stratification of patients with resectable PDAC undergoing curative-intent surgery

## CA 19-9: High-Risk Threshold
- Ushida et al. stratified patients using 500 U per mL threshold
- Both anatomical resectability and CA 19-9 category were independent prognostic factors
- Resectable PDAC with high CA 19-9 showed worse survival than resectable with low levels
- Comparable survival to borderline resectable disease suggests potential indication for NAT

## CA 19-9: Limitations
- Not specific to PDAC; elevated in biliary obstruction and cholangitis
- Should be measured after adequate biliary drainage with bilirubin less than 2.0 mg per dL
- Lewis antigen-negative individuals, 5% to 10% of East Asians, cannot synthesize CA 19-9
- No universally established cutoff; inter-assay variability precludes interchangeability

## 18F-FDG PET/CT: SUVmax Prognosis
- Pretreatment tumor SUVmax greater than 5.5 predicts worse survival after resection
- Pretreatment SUVmax greater than 7.5 associated with worse outcomes after NAT
- Evidence supporting tumor SUVmax as prognostic marker remains limited
- Additional well-designed large-scale studies warranted

## Multivariable Risk Models: Overview
- Pretreatment risk stratification clinically relevant for resectable PDAC
- Both upfront resection and NAT are valid treatment options
- Models developed to predict early recurrence or death following upfront resection
- Multiple representative preoperative models published

## Table 2: Nakamura et al. 2018
- Primary outcome: Overall survival
- Predictors: Tumor location in head, tumor size greater than 2 cm on CT, serum CA 19-9 greater than 100 U per mL
- Application: Patient stratification according to overall survival
- Early model establishing baseline preoperative risk assessment

## Table 2: Kim et al. 2020
- Primary outcome: Recurrence-free survival
- Predictors: CT variables including tumor size, portal venous phase density, necrosis, peripancreatic infiltration, suspicious metastatic lymph nodes
- C-index of 0.68 in temporal validation
- Purely imaging-based risk score approach

## Table 2: Crippa et al. 2024
- Primary outcome: Futile pancreatectomy defined as death or recurrence within 6 months
- Predictors: Tumor size on CT, serum CA 19-9 level, American Society of Anesthesiology class
- C-index of 0.65 in external validation
- Focus on preventing non-beneficial surgery

## Table 2: Jeong et al. 2024
- Primary outcome: Recurrence-free survival
- Predictors: Tumor size on CT, tumor SUVmax on PET/CT, serum CA 19-9, suspicious regional lymph node on CT or PET/CT, suspicious metastasis on PET/CT
- C-index of 0.61 in temporal validation
- Multimodality approach incorporating metabolic imaging

## Table 2: Schouten et al. 2024
- Primary outcome: Overall survival
- Predictors: Anatomic resectability, serum CA 19-9 level 500 U per mL or greater, ECOG performance status 2 or greater
- Patient stratification according to overall survival using A-B-C factors
- Nationwide validation of comprehensive staging approach

## Treatment Strategy: R0 Resection Rates by Stage
- Data from cohort of 616 patients with PDAC
- Among patients undergoing upfront resection: R0 rates 73% resectable, 55% borderline, 16% locally advanced
- When all patients considered including non-surgical: 71%, 45%, and 4% respectively
- Clear differences in surgical outcomes drive treatment strategy selection

## Borderline and Locally Advanced: NAT Standard
- Introduction of multiagent chemotherapy led to increasing NAT adoption
- For borderline resectable PDAC, NAT associated with higher R0 rates and improved survival versus upfront surgery
- NAT has become standard initial treatment for borderline resectable disease
- Preferred regimens: FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine combined with albumin-bound paclitaxel

## Conversion Surgery After NAT
- Patients without disease progression during NAT should be considered for conversion surgery
- Restaging typically determined through multidisciplinary discussion
- For locally advanced PDAC, systemic chemotherapy with or without stereotactic radiotherapy recommended
- Favorable treatment responders may subsequently undergo surgical resection

## Resectable Disease: Evolving Paradigm
- Traditionally upfront resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy was standard
- Recently NAT increasingly adopted even for resectable PDAC
- Earlier guidelines recommended upfront resection primarily, reserving NAT for high-risk features
- Guidelines updated since 2024 endorse NAT as initial strategy, upfront resection only for patients without high-risk features

## Unresolved Issues in Resectable PDAC
- NAT implementation remains variable across institutions in real-world practice
- Upfront resection continues to be performed for resectable and even borderline resectable PDAC
- In Korea, multiagent NAT for potentially resectable PDAC not fully reimbursed by National Health Insurance
- Survival benefit of NAT over upfront resection in purely resectable PDAC remains controversial

## Randomized Trial Evidence Summary
- Trials enrolling both resectable and borderline patients demonstrated superior survival with NAT
- PREOPANC and similar studies showed benefit in mixed cohorts
- NORPACT-1 trial exclusively enrolling resectable PDAC failed to demonstrate survival benefit for NAT
- Current evidence does not fully support NAT preference for resectable PDAC as recommended by NCCN

## Restaging After NAT: Fundamental Challenges
- Curative-intent resection improves survival in borderline and locally advanced PDAC treated with NAT
- Feasibility of conversion surgery must be evaluated in non-progressing patients
- Restaging using CT and MRI more challenging than initial staging
- Associated with lower accuracy in predicting likelihood of R0 resection

## Restaging: Overestimation of Vascular Invasion
- CT and MRI tend to overestimate vascular invasion after NAT
- Imaging cannot reliably distinguish viable tumors from post-treatment fibrosis
- Consequently R0 resection may be achieved after NAT in patients initially classified as borderline or even locally advanced
- Radiological downstaging to resectable disease may not be necessary for surgical candidacy

## Restaging: R0 Resection Rates After NAT
- Ferrone et al. reported R0 in 92% of initial borderline or locally advanced patients
- However radiological downstaging occurred in only 35%
- Recent prospective high-resolution CT study:
  - Upfront R0: 88.7% resectable, 52.4% borderline, 0% locally advanced
  - Post-NAT R0: 90.9% resectable, 76.7% borderline, 25.0% locally advanced
- Higher R0 rates achievable after NAT for advanced categories

## Restaging: Interpreting Residual Contact
- Interpretation of anatomical resectability at initial diagnosis not directly applicable after NAT
- Some borderline or locally advanced patients at restaging may still benefit from curative-intent resection
- Regression of tumor-vessel contact after NAT predicts R0 with high specificity
- Objective tumor response compared to baseline associated with higher R0 likelihood

## Figure 10: Restaging Success with FOLFIRINOX
- 75-year-old man with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer
- Baseline: SMV abutment with deformity, SMA abutment, SUVmax 11.4, CA 19-9 at 51 U per mL
- After six cycles FOLFIRINOX: decreased size, improved SMV contact without residual deformity
- Complete metabolic response on PET/CT with normalized CA 19-9 at 18.4 U per mL

## Figure 10: Surgical Outcome After Restaging
- Residual tumor infiltration persisted along medial pancreatic head abutting SMA
- Despite residual contact, patient underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy
- Achieved margin-negative resection
- Remained recurrence-free for 8 years following surgery

## Restaging: CA 19-9 Response Dynamics
- Normalization or reduction of CA 19-9 by more than 50% from baseline associated with higher R0 rates
- Pattern of changes important for prognosis:
  - Constant or bidirectional reductions to normal levels: best survival
  - Persistently normal or reduction without normalization: intermediate
  - Persistently increasing without normalization: worst survival outcomes

## Restaging: PET/CT Metabolic Response
- Tumor-vessel contact without FDG uptake more likely associated with R0 resection
- Residual contact with persistent FDG uptake less favorable
- Changes in tumor extent, tumor-vessel contact, CA 19-9, and metabolic activity refine interpretation
- In favorable responders, residual contact may not represent true vascular invasion

## Conclusions: Imaging Essentials
- Accurate imaging evaluations essential for diagnosis and management of PDAC
- Pancreatic CT protocol remains cornerstone for tumor staging and resectability assessment
- MRI and PET/CT serve as complementary problem-solving tools
- Systematic reporting facilitates multidisciplinary decision-making

## Conclusions: Evolving Concept of Resectability
- Paradigm evolving from purely anatomical framework to comprehensive approach
- Incorporates tumor biology and patient-related conditional factors
- Combined assessment of anatomical, biological, and conditional factors improves prognostic stratification
- A-B-C approach enables refined risk stratification compared to anatomy alone

## Conclusions: Treatment Selection for Resectable Disease
- For resectable PDAC, both upfront resection and NAT represent viable treatment strategies
- Current evidence remains insufficient to clearly favor one approach over the other
- Future research should focus on identification and validation of robust biomarkers
- Goal is personalized treatment selection and optimization of outcomes

## Conclusions: Restaging After NAT
- Radiological restaging more challenging than initial staging and may overestimate vascular invasion
- Changes in tumor-vessel contact, objective tumor response, and biological factors help address limitations
- Post-treatment CA 19-9 dynamics and PET/CT metabolic response provide incremental value
- Robust criteria required to guide selection of optimal candidates for conversion surgery
